raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old man was admitted to the intensive care unit at Steve Biko  Academic Hospital with acute pancreatitis, suspected clinically based on  a raised amylase level (450 U/L; reference range: 20 - 104 U/L), and later  confirmed on a computed tomography (CT) scan. Pancreatitis was due  to the use of herbal medication and a cytomegalovirus infection (viral  load: 5472 U/L). The patient was HIV co-infected (stage 4 according  to World Health Organization staging guidelines), but highly active  antiretroviral therapy had not been initiated. In addition, he had stage 3  chronic kidney disease (CKD), proven on biopsy to be due to HIV-related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, complicated by anaemia and  secondary hyperparathyroidism. The patient developed severe, acute  hypocalcaemia (corrected serum calcium level: 1.09 mmol/L; reference  range: 2.15 - 2.50 mmol/L), precipitated by pancreatitis-induced  saponification and aggressive administration of saline. Clinically,  this presented as a positive Trousseau's sign during blood pressure  measurement and a prolonged corrected QT (QTc) interval (360 ms) on  the electrocardiograph upon admission (Fig. 1A). The patient became  unexpectedly unstable 24 hours post admission and developed acute  pulmonary oedema that required ventilation. An electrocardiogram  performed at this time revealed ST elevation in keeping with an acute  myocardial infarction (Fig. 1B). Serum troponins were initially within  the normal range (40 ng/L), but later became markedly elevated (peak:  4 358 ng/L). His urine output remained >1 mL/kg/h. 
 An acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction was diagnosed and  a thrombolytic agent was prescribed, while intravenous calcium  replacement had been initiated as part of his resuscitation. The patient  stabilised before the thrombolytic agent could be administered, with  complete resolution of the ST elevation and no residual Q waves (Fig. 1C). 
 The thrombolytic agent was not given subsequently. The patient made  an uneventful recovery and was discharged to the ward 5 days later. 
 Various investigations were conducted in relation to the cardiac insult.  A technetium sestamibi scan of the patient's myocardium revealed no  perfusion defects (Fig. 2), whereas a non-contrast CT scan of the chest  revealed no coronary artery calcification or plaques. A cardiac magnetic  resolution imaging (MRI) scan revealed normal coronary arteries,  with no areas of stenosis and no bridging myocardium. A coronary  angiogram was contraindicated owing to the patient's CKD.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old man was admitted to the intensive care unit with acute pancreatitis complicated by severe acute hypocalcemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with clinical features of acute pancreatitis following herbal medication use and was admitted to the ICU, where he exhibited a positive Trousseau's sign on blood pressure cuff inflation and subsequently developed acute hemodynamic instability and acute pulmonary edema requiring mechanical ventilation 24 hours after admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: WHO stage 4 HIV infection (antiretroviral therapy-naive) and biopsy-proven HIV-related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis causing stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD), complicated by anemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. History of herbal medication ingestion.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for symptoms of acute pancreatitis and acute dyspnea/pulmonary edema at 24 hours; recent herbal medication use; no prior HAART.

objective.physical_examination: Positive Trousseau's sign elicited during blood pressure measurement on admission. At 24 hours post-admission, became hemodynamically unstable with clinical signs of acute pulmonary edema requiring mechanical ventilation; urine output remained >1 mL/kg/h.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated serum amylase 450 U/L (reference range 20-104 U/L), severe acute hypocalcemia with corrected serum calcium 1.09 mmol/L (reference range 2.15-2.50 mmol/L), initial serum troponin normal at 40 ng/L followed by marked elevation peaking at 4,358 ng/L. Admission ECG showed prolonged QTc interval (360 ms); 24-hour ECG showed acute ST-segment elevation consistent with STEMI, which completely resolved without residual Q waves following IV calcium replacement.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT confirmed acute pancreatitis. Quantitative CMV viral load was 5,472 U/L. Subsequent cardiac workup including technetium-99m sestamibi myocardial perfusion scan (no perfusion defects), non-contrast chest CT (no coronary artery calcification or plaques), and cardiac MRI (normal coronary arteries without stenosis or myocardial bridging) excluded obstructive coronary artery disease (coronary angiography contraindicated due to CKD).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with acute pancreatitis secondary to cytomegalovirus (CMV) co-infection (confirmed by CMV viral load 5,472 U/L) and herbal medication toxicity in an ART-naive WHO stage 4 HIV patient, complicated by severe acute hypocalcemia (1.09 mmol/L from pancreatic saponification and saline resuscitation) inducing coronary artery spasm and transient pseudo-STEMI with acute pulmonary edema. Prompt intravenous calcium replacement and mechanical ventilation stabilized the patient with complete ST-segment resolution prior to thrombolysis (thrombolytic withheld); normal coronary arteries were confirmed on cardiac MRI, non-contrast chest CT, and sestamibi scan. Discharged to the general ward after 5 days following an uneventful recovery.
